newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn stands by plans for Transrapid train.
newsitem.headline: Bonn stands by plans for Transrapid train.

text.p: German Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann on Wednesday parried critics of the controversial Transrapid magnetic levitation train, but said the government would keep a close eye to prevent cost overruns.
Wissmann told parliament's transport committee Bonn would stand by its plans for the high-speed rail project.
Critics claim business projections for the planned Hamburg-Berlin route are too optimistic, and that it will damage the environment.

The northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, through which the route would pass, on Tuesday filed a suit in the Constitutional Court to block construction, which is due to begin in 1998 and be completed in 2005.

In remarks prepared for delivery to the committee, Wissmann did not respond directly to the suit, but said: "The federal government maintains its great interest in seeing that this high-technology project, so important for our economy and for Germany itself, is successfully realised."
"But as I have always said, there will not be a Transrapid at any price, only one that is convincing in both its technical and its economic dimensions."
Wissmann declined to update the cost projections, saying a new study of the project's viability would be ready by April.
In the past, the government has committed 5.6 billion marks ($3.5 billion) for the Hamburg-Berlin track, leaving private-sector partners to pay the rest of the estimated nine billion mark bill.

"Cost developments must remain within an objectively justifiable range of the original financing plan of the private partners," Wissmann said. "We will look very critically at excessive price increases."
But critics say the costs will inevitably be far higher, making the project unviable. They say that taxpayers will be stuck with the bill.
The Verkehrsclub Deutschland, which represents automobile drivers, called the Transrapid a fiscal "time bomb" whose costs would explode, damaging the federal budget.

Professor Rolf Kreibich of the Institute for Future Studies and Technology Evaluation criticised the Transrapid as a hole that would absorb billions of marks and never turn a profit, as it could not attract the number of passengers projected.
"There is no cost-effective and conclusive model for the Transrapid," Kreibich told German television.
Foreign planners are not interested in the technology, which has also not been integrated into European mass transport plans, Kreibich said.

Hans-Christoph Atzpodien, chief executive of the company planning the train, replied there was a list of countries interested in buying the Transrapid, which represents an effective alternative to domestic air travel.
Thyssen Transrapid System GmbH, one of the partners in the project, said in a statement, "All participants have a natural interest in seeing that the project is viable.

"Neither Thyssen nor the other companies involved can affod to invest money in a project that does not allow us to expect a sustainable return. This means security for the federal government's investment as well."
Other partners are Siemens AG, ADtranz, Hochtief AG, Philipp Holzmann AG, Bilfinger & Berger Bau AG and Deutsche Bahn AG. -- Bonn newsroom, 49 228 26097150 ($1=1.5978 Mark)
